questions.heading: Those Products Are What a GPU Does Best
questions.stem: A team's LP has 50 million nonzeros, and they plan to run PDLP on a GPU. Which property of each PDHG iteration lets its work spread over the card's thousands of cores?

options.text: It factorizes the matrix once, and each factor's columns run in parallel
options.says: PDHG never factorizes anything; a factorization is a chain of dependent steps that does not split cleanly across cores.

options.text: Each row of Ax and each clip is computed without the other rows
options.says: Right: an iteration is products with A and A-transposed plus element-wise clips, and every row's sum is independent.

options.text: It reads only one row of the matrix, so each core holds very little
options.says: An iteration reads every nonzero twice, once for Ax and once for A-transposed y.

options.text: It solves the dual exactly, and that dual splits into one part per core
options.says: PDHG never solves for the prices exactly: each iteration moves them by one dual step, and the next starts from there.

questions.heading: A First-Order Method Stops at a Tolerance, Not at a Vertex
questions.stem: PDLP solves a budget LP at tolerance 1e-6 and reports OPTIMAL. The budget rows hold thousands of $k each. Which of these can the returned plan still do?

options.text: Return a basis, so the plan can seed a simplex warm start
options.says: PDLP returns no basis; a model that needs one needs a simplex solve or a crossover.

options.text: Miss the optimal objective by about one percent
options.says: At 1e-6 the objective was within 8.2e-7 of the simplex optimum, relatively, far closer than one percent.

options.text: Break a budget row by a small fraction of a $k
options.says: Right: at 1e-6 the plan broke a row by 0.012, allowed because the test is relative to all the row bounds together.

options.text: Keep every budget row exactly, since OPTIMAL means no breach
options.says: OPTIMAL for PDLP means within the tolerance; at 1e-6 a row was broken by 0.012.

questions.heading: Plain PDHG Stalls on GridCap's Numbers; Rescaling Rescues It
questions.stem: A crew LP has rows in hours, with entries near 1, and rows in dollars, with entries near 10,000. Plain PDHG with equal constant steps stalls far from the optimum. Which change attacks the cause?

options.text: Raise the iteration limit tenfold, so the hour rows have time to settle
options.says: The stall does not end with more iterations: as built, the GridCap run was 13% off at 1,000 and still 13% off at 100,000.

options.text: Shrink both steps, so the dollar rows with large entries are not overshot
options.says: The steps are already tiny because the largest entries set them; that is the stall's cause, not its cure.

options.text: Raise both steps, so the hour rows with entries near 1 move faster
options.says: With the entries as built, steps raised that far break the convergence condition many times over; the large entries are what cap them.

options.text: Scale each row and column, so the dollar rows' entries come near 1
options.says: Right: rescaling brought GridCap's entries to between 0.24 and 1, and its steps were then 1,500 times larger and reached 4.8e-6.
